body_markdown:
Last year, over 8.41M vehicles rolled out of factories in Japan, according to[OICA](https://oica.net/auto-industry-growth-shifted-east-in-2025-amid-global-repositioning/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) data. That puts Japan third among the car-building nations, behind the U.S. (10.2M) and China (34.5M), but ahead of India (6.5M) and Germany (4.1M).


Compared to the rapid rise of India and China, Japan is an established power in the car world with decades of rich history and heritage, plus a rich catalog of cars and trucks that boasted groundbreaking designs, shook up the entire industry, or both. Which means there are plenty of vintage Japanese vehicles that appeal to enthusiasts and collectors, obviously. But the car industry in Japan is also much younger than the ones in Europe and the United States, and therefore so is its history.


The most desirable and valuable Japanese cars, compared to their Western equivalents, are both much newer and, at least for now, much less valuable.


The graph above looks at the top 20 worldwide auction sales for cars from the major manufacturers of enthusiast vehicles. The top dogs from France, for example, mostly come from the prewar years, which makes sense given the golden age of Bugatti and the coachbuilt concours stars from Delahaye, Talbot-Lago, etc. Most of Italy’s top cars, meanwhile, come from the age of[Ferrari 250 GTOs](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/250_gto/1962/1962-ferrari-250_gto-si?id=aCn1I000000CwcWSAS) and[Cal Spiders](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ferrari/250_california/1963/1963-ferrari-250_california-swb?id=aCn1I000000CxXHSA0) , while America’s most valuable come from the muscle car era. Japan’s golden age, by contrast, is much, much newer, as most of its top 20 cars were built after 2000.


The *most* valuable Japanese cars are also a lot *less* valuable than the Western ones. If you added up the prices of the 20 most expensive Japanese cars ever sold, you’d get $28M. All those combined is still millions less than the single top German, Italian, American, or British car. Japan’s top-20 list is also the only one that includes online sales, which, in general, tend to move newer and less-expensive cars than the higher-end live auctions.


Although European classics have been selling for seven figures since the ’80s, a Japanese car didn’t cross the $1M mark until 2013, when a Toyota 2000GT sold at auction for[$1,155,000](https://rmsothebys.com/auctions/dd13/lots/r153-1967-toyota-2000gt/) . In the 2000s, 2000GTs typically sold in the mid-$100K range, so crossing the $1M threshold caused quite a stir and cemented the idea that Japanese cars could indeed be top-tier collectibles. All to say, the very concept of a top-shelf Japanese car is relatively new, and it’s a market segment that’s still maturing.
